quote: The answer is that the proper generalization is “Emeralds are green.” I’m not going to go into the arguments at the moment. It is not the subject of this essay, and the obvious answer in this case happens to be correct.
content: Goodman’s riddle is not an eccentric puzzle to be waved past; it is the demonstration that “simplest generalization” has no content until a vocabulary is chosen, since “green” is as gruesome relative to the grue-bleen basis as “grue” is relative to ours, and Book III’s annotations found the same gap at the centre of “simple boundaries in Thingspace.” The essay’s whole argument is that many-worlds is “the simplest generalization that fits all known facts,” and the sentence that declines to say what makes a generalization simple is the sentence on which the argument depends. Solomonoff induction, the sequence’s formal answer, resolves grue only relative to a reference machine, as the annotation on Decoherence Is Simple records. “The true Way is not stupid” is not an argument; it is the statement that the author already knows which generalization is right, which is what Goodman’s riddle was designed to expose.

quote: If we try to get probabilities by counting the number of distinct observers, then there is no obvious reason why the integrated squared modulus of the wavefunction should correlate with statistical experimental results. There is no known reason for the Born probabilities
content: This admission undoes the ranking the essay is about to make. The evidence for quantum mechanics is entirely statistical: frequencies of detector clicks matching squared moduli. A theory that does not yield those frequencies has not yet reproduced the evidence, and “unitary evolution plus decoherence” does not yield them; the essay says so. To reach experiment, Everett needs either a Born postulate, which is an extra law of the kind the essay counts against collapse, or the decision-theoretic derivation the essay is “rather suspicious” of. Hanson’s mangled-worlds proposal (Hanson (2003)) was never developed further and has no adherents. So the comparison “many-worlds wins outright” is between a theory with an unexplained Born rule and a theory with an unexplained collapse rule that carries the Born rule inside it, and the essay’s Occam accounting charges the second for its rule and the first for nothing. Opus’s annotation records that the Born problem is unsolved; the annotator adds that it is unsolved at the one place where the theory meets the data, so that “the simplest theory that fits all known facts” is, at present, a theory that fits the facts only with an addition it cannot justify.

quote: Much worse, any physical scenario in which there was a single surviving world, so that any measurement had only a single outcome, would violate Special Relativity.
content: This is a “fully general objection” with published counterexamples. Bell’s theorem shows that single-outcome theories must be nonlocal in the sense that the outcome statistics cannot be explained by local variables; it does not show that they violate special relativity, since no-signalling holds and the relevant question is whether the theory’s dynamics can be made Lorentz-invariant. Relativistic collapse models exist: Tumulka’s flash version of GRW has a Lorentz-invariant law for the distribution of flashes (Tumulka (2006)), and relativistic continuous spontaneous localization was constructed by Bedingham et al. (2014); in them measurements have single outcomes, no preferred frame is needed for the predictions, and nothing travels faster than light. The essay’s picture of a single world as requiring a global “now” confuses two things: a block universe is a single world and is the standard relativistic picture, and what Bell forbids is a local explanation of the correlations, not the singleness of the world. Everett evades Bell by denying that measurements have single outcomes, and whether it is thereby local is disputed among Everettians (Wallace and Timpson for; Maudlin against). The essay treats one horn as a violation of physics and the other as free; the physics ranks neither.

quote: Incidentally, this experiment has already been performed, and if there is a mysterious influence it would have to travel six million times as fast as light in the reference frame of the Swiss Alps.
content: The number is right and the source, which the essay omits, is Scarani, Tittel, Zbinden & Gisin (2000), who used the Geneva fibre-optic Bell tests to bound the speed of any hypothetical influence at more than 2/3 × 107 c in the frame of the Swiss Alps; a later experiment with the detectors in relative motion (Zbinden et al. (2001)) showed the correlations survive when each measurement is “first” in its own frame, which is the second fact the essay reports. Those are real results and the essay’s use of them is fair. What they show is that no theory in which one measurement causes the other by a signal in a preferred frame can be right; they do not decide between Everett, pilot-wave theory (in which the nonlocal connection is not a signal), and relativistic collapse, all of which reproduce them. The experiments the sequence cites correctly are the experiments that fail to discriminate the interpretations, which is the situation the sequence exists to deny.

quote: The only reason why many-worlds is not universally acknowledged as a direct prediction of physics which requires magic to violate, is that a contingent accident of our Earth’s scientific history gave an entrenched academic position to a phlogiston-like theory that had an unobservable faster-than-light magical “collapse” devouring all other worlds.
content: The fourteen essays of this sequence never mention the de Broglie–Bohm pilot-wave theory. It is realist, single-world, deterministic, has no collapse and no observer-dependence, reproduces every prediction of quantum mechanics, has decoherence as a derived phenomenon rather than an interpretation, and was endorsed by Bell as the account that should be taught. Its costs are nonlocality (which Bell’s theorem imposes on any single-world theory, and which the flash and CSL models above show is compatible with relativistic statistics) and a preferred foliation in its relativistic extensions. Against the essay’s list of what a single-world theory must be, non-linear, non-unitary, discontinuous, acausal, informal, pilot-wave theory is none of these. So the “one best guess” was selected from a menu of two, the second item being a caricature, and the sentence about the “only reason” many-worlds is not universally acknowledged omits the reason that the physicist who proved Bell’s theorem gave: there is another realist theory with fewer open problems at the point where theory meets data. A reader who wants to check the sequence’s verdict should read Bell’s Speakable and Unspeakable in Quantum Mechanics (1987), which defends realism, decoherence and the seriousness of the measurement problem, and reaches a different best guess. Phlogiston, for the record, appears here for what Book I’s annotations counted as at least the eighth time in the book, and the analogy fails as before: collapse theories make predictions and are being tested.
